rationale: Both record Judah's children in a Canaanite marriage, name Er and Onan, and say the evil firstborn Er was put to death by God. The target's wording of Shua's relationship and Shelon/Shelah remain distinct.

Both explicitly locate Caleb as Eseron's son; the source's additional Gazouba, Jerioth, and offspring wording is retained without changing its relationships or identifying this Caleb with other Calebs.
The scribal families dwelling at Jabes continue the target's unfinished named family list after Solomon's sons; their Kinaians origin and Rechab-house statement remain the source's own particulars.
These names close the additional Jerusalem sons after the target's four by Bersabee. The source's own 'nine' applies to this continuation; repeated names are not merged.
The target continues the source's unfinished named family enumeration and then explicitly describes that group as potters who grew strong with the king in his kingdom.

The source's discovery of rich, good pasture answers the target's explicit journey to seek pasture for the same particular group's livestock; the source adds the former inhabitants and peaceful condition.

Both connect Reubenite territorial dwelling with abundant livestock: the target requests land nourishing livestock, and the source explains eastward dwelling by numerous livestock. Their particular place names are retained without independently mapping them.
The source's 'Their enrollment, all of them' dates the target's particular named Gadite men, seven brethren, ancestry, and settlements; it does not assign every named man a ruler's office.

The source names the particular half-Manasseh settlement and its growth; the target's 'These were the chiefs of their ancestral houses' supplies that group's seven named leaders without mapping differently spelled places to another book.

Both refer to Solomon building the house in Jerusalem. The source locates Azariah's priestly service there; the target calls it the Lord's house and describes the singers' ministry until its construction.

Both explicitly identify Caleb as son of Jephonne. The source lists his descendants; the target records the city's plains and villages given to him. This does not identify him with other Caleb families.
